public_rationale: He said that with Nvidia pulling back and SoftBank possibly following, other investors would be skittish. Nvidia did walk back its $100 billion figure (e4). But on Feb 27, two weeks after the post, Nvidia and SoftBank each committed $30 billion, and Amazon committed $50 billion, to a $110 billion round (e1). By March 31 the round had grown to $122 billion, including $3 billion from new individual investors (e2). So the retreat he expected did not happen, and new money still came in. Secondary-market demand for OpenAI shares did weaken in March (e3). But reports linked that to Anthropic's appeal and to valuation, not to Nvidia or SoftBank. On the plain reading, the predicted investor flight did not occur.
limitations: 'Skittish' is vague. On a looser reading that counts secondary-market softness, the claim gets partial support (e3).
Part of the round was conditional or staged (for example, part of Amazon's money), and the sources do not show how much was actually paid in.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: because Nvidia backed away from its $100 billion plan and SoftBank might do the same, other investors, especially new ones, would hold back from putting money into OpenAI in the months after the post.
The clearest test is OpenAI's funding round, which was open at the time of the post. Did outside investors join it, or did it stall, shrink, or lose backers?
Secondary-market demand for OpenAI shares is relevant too. But it supports the claim only if the hesitation was linked to Nvidia or SoftBank.
criteria.support_condition: Reports after 2026-02-13 that OpenAI's round stalled, shrank, or failed to draw new investors, or that investors held back over Nvidia's or SoftBank's retreat.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Nvidia and SoftBank themselves invest heavily soon after the post, and OpenAI's round closes at or above its target with new outside investors joining.
